Rust's iterator chain is not a convenience — it is the idiomatic way to write loops, and it compiles to the same machine code as a hand-written for with bounds checks removed.

The standard collections

Type Use for Lookup Order
Vec<T> a growable list O(1) index insertion
VecDeque<T> push/pop both ends O(1) ends insertion
HashMap<K, V> key → value, unordered O(1) avg none
BTreeMap<K, V> key → value, sorted O(log n) sorted by key
HashSet<T> / BTreeSet<T> membership O(1) / O(log n) none / sorted
String UTF-8 text — —
BinaryHeap<T> priority queue O(log n) push/pop max-heap

Default choice: Vec for sequences, HashMap for maps. Switch to BTreeMap when you need ordered iteration or a deterministic output (tests, serialisation, reports).

Vec<T>

Slices

Rule of thumb: take &[T] in function parameters, never &Vec<T>. The slice accepts both and does not tie you to a Vec.

HashMap

Keys need Eq + Hash. f64 does not work — use an integer, a string, or a newtype with a manual Hash impl over the bit pattern.

HashMap with a non-string key

Deterministic iteration

HashMap iteration order is randomised per process (HashDoS protection). Tests that print a map are flaky. Use BTreeMap, or collect and sort:

BTreeMap and BTreeSet

VecDeque and BinaryHeap

Iterators

An iterator is anything with next(). The Iterator trait has ~70 provided methods, all built on next.

The three iteration forms

Lazy by default

Iterator adapters do nothing until something consumes them:

This is why chaining is free: map().filter().take(10) on a million elements only touches as many as take needs.

The adapters you will actually use

Adapter Effect
map transform each item
filter keep items matching a predicate
filter_map transform + drop None in one step
flat_map transform to an iterator, flatten
take(n) / skip(n) limit
take_while / skip_while limit by predicate
enumerate (index, item)
zip pair two iterators
chain concatenate
rev reverse (needs DoubleEndedIterator)
peekable look ahead without consuming
step_by(n) every nth
scan stateful map
inspect side effect without changing items
collect build a collection
fold / reduce accumulate
sum / product / count aggregate
any / all / find / position search
min_by_key / max_by_key extremes
sort_by_key (on Vec) order
group_by (itertools) group runs

collect into anything

The Result<Vec<_>, _> collect is a workhorse: it stops at the first error and returns it, which is exactly the semantics you want when parsing a list of rows.

fold and reduce

Custom iterators

Implement Iterator and you get all 70 methods free.

Streaming files without loading them

BufReader batches syscalls. Reading a file with unbuffered read_line is 10–100× slower. For maximum throughput on large files, memchr-based crates or bstr are worth reaching for.

Exercises

  1. Given Vec<(String, u32)> of (name, score), produce the top 3 by score using one iterator chain and collect.
  2. Write fn group_by_first_letter(words: &[&str]) -> BTreeMap<char, Vec<&str>>.
  3. Implement Iterator for a struct that yields every other element of a slice.
  4. Convert a Vec<String> of numbers to Result<Vec<i64>, ParseIntError> with one collect call.
  5. Count word frequencies in a 10 MB file with BufReader and compare timing against fs::read_to_string. Explain the difference.
  6. Replace this with a single chain: build a HashMap<&str, usize> of counts, then filter to counts > 1, then collect keys into a sorted Vec.
